faq.a: Alveoli are tiny air sacs at the ends of the smallest airways in your lungs. Each is wrapped in capillaries, and this is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.

faq.q: How does oxygen get into the blood?
faq.a: By diffusion. There is more oxygen in the air in an alveolus than in the blood flowing past, so oxygen moves across the thin wall into the blood, where red blood cells pick it up.

faq.q: Why are the alveolus walls so thin?
faq.a: Gases have to cross them by diffusion, which is only fast over very short distances. The wall and the capillary next to it together are about a thousandth of a millimetre thick.
asks: Tell me about the thin wall

faq.q: Why do lungs have so many alveoli?
faq.a: Lots of small sacs give a much bigger surface than one big bag. The total surface in adult lungs is roughly the size of a badminton court, so a lot of gas can cross at once.
asks: How big is the surface of the lungs?

faq.q: What does the red blood cell do in the lungs?
faq.a: It contains haemoglobin, a protein that grabs oxygen in the lungs and lets it go in the body's tissues. It also helps carry some carbon dioxide back to the lungs.
asks: Tell me about the red blood cell

facts: Adult lungs contain roughly 300 to 500 million alveoli.
The barrier between air and blood in an alveolus is about 0.5 to 1 micrometre thick.
The total gas exchange surface of adult lungs is commonly estimated at about 50 to 100 square metres.
